draft.title: Supplements
card: A supplement is a product taken in addition to normal food to try to improve health or performance. Examples are caffeine, creatine and protein powder.
a stimulant that may reduce the feeling of effort and help some athletes in endurance or alertness tasks. It can also cause a racing heart, jitters and poor sleep.
a substance stored in muscle that may help some athletes in short, high intensity efforts such as sprints. It can cause weight gain from water and stomach upset in some people.
Supplements may help some athletes but not all. Many are not tested for safety or purity, so a product may contain less, more or something other than what the label says.
draft.remember: Supplements may help some athletes, but they carry risks and the contents are not always checked.

a.q: Why should an athlete be careful when choosing a supplement?
opts: Contents may not be tested, so the label could be wrong
Supplements always work, so any dose is safe to take
Supplements work the same for every athlete who takes them
Supplements are only a risk when taken before sleep
a.why: Many supplements are not tested for safety or purity, so the label may not match what is inside. The option saying they always work is wrong because the card says they may help only some athletes.
a.clue: Think about what is checked before a product is sold.

b.q: Jade, a 17-year-old sprinter in Newcastle, wants to take creatine because her teammate says it made her faster. Which response is best supported?
opts: It may help short sprints for some, but it has risks
It will help her, because it helped her teammate
It is useless, as it only helps endurance athletes
It is safe, because supplements are tested for purity
b.why: Creatine may help some athletes in short, high intensity efforts, but results differ between people and it can have side effects. Assuming it will work for Jade because it worked for her teammate is tempting, but supplements do not affect every athlete the same way.
b.clue: One person's result does not decide how it works for another.

a.best: Contents may not be tested, so the label could be wrong

b.best: It may help short sprints for some, but it has risks

proposal.title: Supplements
card: A supplement is a product taken in addition to normal food to try to improve health or performance. Examples are caffeine, creatine and protein powder.
a stimulant that may reduce the feeling of effort and help some athletes in endurance or alertness tasks. It can also cause a racing heart, jitters and poor sleep.
a substance stored in muscle that may help some athletes in short, high intensity efforts such as sprints. It can cause weight gain from water and stomach upset in some people.

Many supplements are not tested for safety or purity, so a product may contain less, more or something other than its label says. Australian sports guidance advises athletes under 18 to avoid performance supplements such as caffeine and creatine.

a.q: Which statement about supplements is supported by the card?
opts: Many are not tested, so contents can differ from the label
Many are tested, so contents can be trusted to match labels
Caffeine can improve sleep, so it suits evening sessions
Creatine can help long endurance events more than sprints
a.why: Many supplements are not tested for safety or purity, so what is inside may not match the label. The option saying contents can be trusted is tempting, but testing is not required for many products, so a label is no guarantee.
